topic: framing and straightening the roof of a small timber workshop

provenance.author: subagent-en-b
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is measurement arithmetic and cutting lists, base is a diagnostic conversation about a sagging ridge

a: Here are six rafters cut for the workshop roof, measured this morning with a steel tape.
The lengths are three point one, two point eight, three point four, three point one, two point nine, and three point three metres.
Sort them from longest to shortest and tell me the difference between the two extremes.
Then convert each length to millimetres and mark which ones differ from three point two metres.
Finish with the mean length of the six rafters, rounded to the nearest millimetre.
base: We are framing a roof over the workshop and the ridge line is visibly out of true.
The building is six metres long and the ridge sags perhaps twenty millimetres near the middle.
All the rafters came from the same batch of timber and were cut on the same day.
The wall plates looked level when we set them, at least by the spirit level we had.
What would you check first before we start packing anything out with shims?

a: Longest to shortest gives three point four, three point three, three point one, three point one metres.
Then two point nine and two point eight metres, with an extreme difference of six hundred millimetres.
In millimetres that is three thousand four hundred, three thousand three hundred, then three thousand one hundred twice.
Then two thousand nine hundred and two thousand eight hundred millimetres, all measured along the top edge.
Every rafter differs from three thousand two hundred millimetres, and the mean is three thousand one hundred millimetres.
base: Start with the wall plates again, because a spirit level over six metres hides a great deal.
Run a taut string from end to end and measure down to the plate every metre.
A sag in the ridge usually begins in the plates rather than in the rafters themselves.
Check the birdsmouth cuts too, since a deep seat cut drops that rafter by its own depth.
Are the birdsmouths all cut to the same depth, or were they marked one by one?

a: Next batch: I need collar ties at one third of the rafter length down from the ridge.
Give me that distance for each of the six rafters, rounded to the nearest five millimetres.
Then list the six ties from longest to shortest with their cut lengths in millimetres.
Assume each tie spans one point eight metres across at that height on every pair.
Add fifty millimetres to every tie for the overlap at both ends of the timber.
base: The birdsmouths were marked one at a time against the plate, by two different people.
That would explain a great deal, because nobody worked to one single set-out line.
We have no string line long enough, though there is a laser somewhere in the van.
The plates were bedded on mortar and the mortar was not perfectly even along the top.
How much variation in seat depth would actually show up as twenty millimetres at the ridge?

a: One third down from the ridge, rounded to five millimetres, is one thousand one hundred thirty-five for the longest.
Then one thousand one hundred, one thousand thirty-five twice, nine hundred sixty-five, and nine hundred thirty-five.
Every collar tie spans one point eight metres, so each cut length is one thousand eight hundred fifty millimetres.
With the fifty millimetre overlap included, all six ties come out identical in length.
Cut six pieces at one thousand eight hundred fifty millimetres and label them by rafter position.
base: A seat cut two millimetres deep changes that rafter's height by the same two millimetres.
Twenty millimetres of sag is therefore not seat depth alone; something else is adding to it.
Look at the ridge board itself, which may well be sagging between its own supports.
A thin ridge board over six metres will bow under the weight of the rafters.
What section is the ridge, and how many props are holding it at the moment?

a: Correction on the third rafter: it is three point zero five metres, not three point one.
Recalculate only its millimetre length, its position in the sorted list, and the new mean.
Leave the collar ties alone since they do not depend on the rafter lengths.
Then give me the total running metres of timber for all six rafters together.
Add ten percent for waste and round the result up to the next whole metre.
base: The ridge is a plain board, thirty-two by two hundred, with props at each end only.
Nothing holds it in the middle apart from the rafters that lean against it.
It sounded fine when we planned it, since the whole span is only six metres.
Now that I look along it from the gable, the bow is obvious in daylight.
Would a single prop in the middle be enough to take that bow out?

a: Three point zero five metres is three thousand fifty millimetres, below both three thousand one hundred rafters.
The sorted order becomes three thousand four hundred, three thousand three hundred, three thousand one hundred, three thousand fifty.
Then two thousand nine hundred and two thousand eight hundred millimetres at the bottom of the list.
The new mean is eighteen thousand five hundred fifty divided by six, or three thousand ninety-two millimetres.
Total timber is eighteen point five five metres, or twenty-one metres after ten percent waste.
base: A single central prop will help, but the ridge board is the wrong section for that span.
Thirty-two millimetres on edge is thin, and it is carrying thrust from both slopes.
I would prop it now, then sister a second board alongside once the load is off.
Do the packing at the plates only after the ridge is straight and properly held.
Have you fixed the rafters at the ridge yet, or are they still just nailed loosely?

a: Now the battens: the roof needs battens at three hundred fifty millimetre centres up each slope.
The slope length is two point eight metres from plate to ridge on both sides.
Tell me how many batten rows fit on one slope and the leftover distance at the top.
Then double it for both slopes and give me the total number of rows.
Each row is six metres long, so give me the running metres of batten as well.
base: The rafters are nailed at the ridge already, two skew nails into the board each side.
Pulling them off would take most of a day and probably split a few ends.
There is also the matter of the tiles, which are stacked on the scaffold now.
We wanted to load out this week while the weather is still holding dry.
Can the propping and sistering be done with the rafters left where they are?

a: Two thousand eight hundred divided by three hundred fifty gives exactly eight rows per slope.
There is no leftover distance, since the spacing divides the slope length without a remainder.
Both slopes together therefore take sixteen rows of batten from the plate to the ridge.
At six metres each, that is ninety-six running metres of batten for the whole roof.
Order in five metre lengths and allow for joints, which adds roughly another ten metres.
base: Yes, all of it can be done from below with the rafters left in place.
Prop the ridge from the floor with an adjustable prop and a spreader on top.
Sister the new board on one side and bolt through at every second rafter.
Then pack the plates where the string shows a dip, using slate or hardwood shims.
Do not load the tiles until the ridge line reads straight along its whole length.

a: Give me a cutting list for the sistering board in three lengths that fit the van.
The board must total six metres and the van takes nothing over two point five metres.
Use equal lengths if possible and tell me the joint positions along the ridge.
The props stand at zero and six metres, so keep joints away from those points.
List each piece with its length and its start and end position on the ridge.
base: That order makes sense and the prop is already in the van from the last job.
I will get the string line up first thing and mark the dips on the plate.
The shims are the part I am least sure about, since slate can crush over time.
We have oak offcuts as well, though they are only about ten millimetres thick.
Which of the two would you use under a plate carrying the whole roof load?

a: Three pieces of two metres each give six metres and fit the van comfortably.
Joints then fall at two metres and four metres along the ridge, clear of both props.
Piece one runs from zero to two metres, piece two from two to four metres.
Piece three runs from four to six metres, finishing at the far prop position.
Stagger the bolts either side of each joint so no joint sits on a single fixing.
base: Use the oak, cut into pads about a hundred millimetres square under each dip.
Slate is fine in thin single leaves but it splits once you stack several together.
Oak takes the load across the grain without crushing, which is what you want here.
Bed each pad on a little mortar so it seats evenly against the wall top.
Then check the string again before anything else goes on top of the plate.
